title: The yoke, the cloth and the net
where: *Agamemnon*: the first chorus, the king’s return, the murder
about: Agamemnon, king of Argos, has been ten years at the war with Troy. In the first passage the chorus of old men sing of how it began: the fleet lay windbound at Aulis, a seer said the goddess Artemis asked for the life of the king’s daughter, and the king spoke. In the second he has just come home, and his wife Clytemnestra has ordered purple cloths spread between his chariot and the door. In the third she stands over his body and tells the old men what she did.

view.says: Agamemnon is Auden’s first example of the Greek tragic situation. Either course is wrong: kill his daughter or fail his army. He could not have avoided the wrong, yet being placed so is the sign of a guilt the gods hold against him: hubris, the self-confidence of a man who believes he is a god, beyond suffering. Sometimes an act shows it: Agamemnon treading the purple carpet.
view.quote: The typical Greek tragic situation is one in which whatever the hero does must be wrong
view.source: “The Greeks and Us” (the introduction to *The Portable Greek Reader*, 1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 19
view.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 946-961 (page 19; the scan drops most punctuation). Read again by the examiner on 2026-10-03: the page number 19 stands at the foot of the page in this scan (line 975), after the paragraph on the tragic hero; the sixteen words quoted are at lines 948-949, and Agamemnon is the first of four examples there. The quoted words were also found, with no punctuation inside them and a dash after the last, in two other scanned copies of the book through the Internet Archive’s full-text search (items forewordsafterwo0000aude and forewordsafterwo00aude)

plates.heading: The king at Aulis, as the elders sing it

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word at the head of clause after clause
lenses.caption: The king names two acts and gives one word to both: Ill to disobey, and ill to kill his child. A word repeated at the head of clauses that follow one another is an anaphora. This one is Aeschylus’s: his Greek begins both clauses with bareia, heavy. Neither act is called the lesser evil. Four lines on, the translator, E. D. A. Morshead, has ’Twixt woe and woe, where the Greek asks which of the two is free of evil. This choice is Auden’s first example of the Greek tragic situation, in which either course is wrong: kill his daughter or fail the army he leads.
lenses.why: The king gives one word to both acts, to disobeying and to killing his child, and calls neither the lesser evil; this is the choice Auden gives first for the Greek tragic situation, in which either course is wrong.

grounds.claim: one word heads both clauses, and woe stands twice in one line
anaphora is a word repeated at the beginning of successive clauses
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), anaphora: repetition of the same word or group of words at the beginning of successive clauses, sentences or lines; Encyclopaedia Britannica, “anaphora”; Online Etymology Dictionary, anaphora (n.)

lenses.label: Metaphor
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.caption: The elders tell what he did in one picture. A yoke is the harness that fastens a pair of oxen. Calling one thing by another’s name is a metaphor: here the compulsion of Fate is a yoke. The yoke is Fate’s and it is compelling. Yet the subject is he and the verb is took. Both are in Aeschylus: his king puts on the yoke-strap of Necessity, and the verb is one used of getting into clothes or armor. Auden wrote that the drama of a play of the Greek kind is in what the situation forces the hero to do, not in what he freely chooses.
lenses.why: The elders’ sentence has a force and an act: the yoke is Fate’s and compels, yet he took it. Auden says the drama of a play of the Greek kind is in what the situation forces the hero to do.

grounds.claim: the yoke is Fate’s and compelling; the subject is he and the verb is took

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The rhyme is the translator’s. Aeschylus’s song is not rhymed. The four lines that name the two acts rhyme by turns: disobey with slay, pride with side. Then dwell ends a line of three beats, and its rhyme waits. Two couplets follow, pairs of rhymed lines. A handbook of verse calls the couplet the simplest group of lines that rhyme holds together, and each of these holds one of the king’s reasons: he dare not desert, and the army’s demand is rightful. Only then does well answer dwell, in the speech’s other line of three beats. So the rhyme left open at the line of the two woes is closed by the prayer that the deed be well.
lenses.why: The translator rhymes the two acts by turns, gives each of the king’s reasons a couplet, and keeps one rhyme waiting, so that the line of the two woes is answered only by the prayer that ends the speech.

grounds.claim: which lines rhyme, which rhyme waits, and that the two lines it joins are the speech’s two lines of three beats (six syllables each; the other eight lines of the speech have eight, nine or twelve)
the Greek song is not rhymed
grounds.source: Agamemnon 205-217 in Smyth’s Greek text: the line-ends follow no scheme of rhyme (lines 205, 211 and 213 end in the same inflection, which is not a rhyme the song is built on); Encyclopaedia Britannica, “rhyme”: rhyme is found only occasionally in classical Greek and Latin poetry

grounds.claim: the couplet is the simplest of the groups of lines that rhyme holds together
grounds.source: Paull F. Baum, The Principles of English Versification (1922), chapter 4, part 2, “The Stanza”, under “Couplet”: lines are used in groups usually held together by rime, and the simplest such group is the couplet (.cache/handbooks/baum-versification-pg21342.txt, lines 3072-3076). The same chapter, under “Short Couplet” (lines 3208-3211), says the quick return of the rime makes the couplet felt as a unit, but that is said of four-beat lines and these couplets are longer, so the caption does not lean on it. Encyclopaedia Britannica, “couplet”: a pair of end-rhymed lines self-contained in grammatical structure and meaning

lenses.caption: Recreant is an old word for one who gives up a fight, and Aeschylus’s word is liponaus, a man who deserts the fleet. Rightfully stands for themis, what custom lays down as right. So both reasons the king gives concern the fleet: to spare the child would be desertion, and the army’s demand is right. Auden describes sparing her as a failure of the king’s duty to the army. Fate’s stands for ananke: force, constraint, necessity. In 1945 Auden called Greek tragedy the tragedy of necessity: what its spectator feels is pity that it had to be so.
lenses.why: The king’s reasons are named in words of duty and law, recreant and rightfully, which is the duty to the army in Auden’s account; and where the translator writes Fate, Aeschylus wrote Necessity, Auden’s own word for Greek tragedy.

plates.heading: At the palace door: thirteen lines

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: stichomythia
lenses.plain: two speakers answer each other a line at a time, often taking up each other’s words
lenses.caption: Queen and king speak one line each for thirteen lines, and she has the first and the last. Talk in single alternating lines is called stichomythia, and the translator keeps Aeschylus’s count. A line takes up what the last one said: unsay is met by I have said, human blame by the murmur of a crowd. Just before, the king refused the cloths as an honor for gods, a pride he fears. In these lines the gods are named once, in her first question. Then the talk is of Priam, of other people, of who wins. After it he walks, the act that for Auden shows his hubris: the self-confidence of a man who believes he is a god.
lenses.why: One line at a time, the talk moves from the gods, his reason for refusing, to Priam, to other people, to who wins; then he does the act Auden names as his hubris.

grounds.claim: thirteen single lines by turns, hers the first and the last; the words taken up; the gods named once
stichomythia: dialogue in alternate single lines, in which the speakers may take up one another’s words

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: Each line is a whole sentence, marked by its kind. In English the queen’s seven are four orders, two questions and one statement. The king’s six are five statements, the first led in by Know, and one question. In his speech just before, the orders are his: Strew not this purple, and bid thee honour me as man. In these lines they are hers, and her last opens on a single word, Yield. His reply ends by saying that his will bows down to hers. Three of her orders are in the Greek, the first and the last among them. Her question about the gods and her order about envy are statements in H. W. Smyth’s Greek text.
lenses.why: In his speech before these lines the orders are the king’s; within them they are the queen’s, while he states and once asks; and after her Yield he says that his will bows down to hers.

lenses.caption: The king calls the talk a war, which is no woman’s part. She answers in his terms: happy victors may well yield in it. He asks if she craves a triumph. In her last line Yield stands for a Greek verb that means be persuaded, or obey. Of thy grace stands for one word, hekon: of your own free will. Her happy victors are in the Greek the fortunate. So her argument is his own good fortune, and what she asks is that he give way freely. Auden wrote that it takes exceptional good fortune to be tempted into hubris.
lenses.why: He calls the talk a war; she answers that the fortunate may yield and asks him to do it freely. Her argument is his good fortune, and Auden says it takes exceptional good fortune to be tempted into hubris.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another; here a robe called a net, after a simile that says it is like one
lenses.caption: The first two lines say she so worked that he could neither flee nor ward off his doom. The next three give the means three ways. First a simile, a likeness said outright with as: a trammel, a fishing net, hemming in a shoal. Then a metaphor, the thing called by another’s name: she trapped him with toils, a hunter’s nets. Only the last line gives the plain noun, a robe. Aeschylus keeps it back in the same way: his Greek names the net first, adds as for fish, and names the garment last.
lenses.why: A simile likens the robe to a net and a metaphor calls it one before it is named, as in Aeschylus’s sentence; and the line before says what it did: he could neither flee nor ward off his doom.

lenses.caption: This translation names a net at nine places, eight of them in the Greek. The first two are thanks for victory: the elders praise the Night that flung a mesh over Troy, and the king says the meshes closed on it by our hands. Each later net is said of the king or his captive Cassandra. One catches no one: rumor, the queen says, gave him more wounds than a net has holes. Cassandra sees one before the murder. Here the queen tells how she used hers; last, the elders mourn their king, wrapped in a spider-web. Auden wrote that the tragic hero starts out glorious and fortunate and ends by suffering more than the chorus that watches him fall.
lenses.why: The picture the elders and the king use, with thanks, for the taking of Troy is the picture of the king’s death, so one image marks the glory Auden says the hero begins in and the suffering he ends in.

grounds.claim: nine places, four speakers, and who is caught at each (at one of the nine, the queen’s comparison for the king’s rumored wounds, no one is caught)

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: From Old French *tramail*, a fine fishing net; the sense of anything that hinders dates from the 1650s.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, trammel (n.)

notes.note: From Latin *inextricabilis*, that cannot be disentangled. The Greek word, *apeiron*, is used in tragedy of garments in which one is entangled past escape.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, inextricable (adj.); Liddell-Scott-Jones, apeiros (B), which cites this line

notes.gloss: nets · from a word for cloth
notes.note: A *toil* is a net or snare for taking prey, from French *toile*, a hunting net, cloth or web, from Latin *tela*, a web. It is now mostly used in the plural.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, toil (n.2)

notes.note: The Greek word is *ploutos*, wealth. At the door the king was loath to waste the wealth of the house by trampling the cloths.
notes.source: Agamemnon 1383 and 949 (Smyth’s text); Liddell and Scott, Intermediate Lexicon, ploutos, which quotes the phrase; agamemnon/p4, rows 41.4 to 41.6

notes.note: A dictionary of the translator’s day gives *baffling* as bewildering, or as defeating skill or effort. The word is his; the Greek has none here.
notes.source: A New English Dictionary, vol. I (1888), Baffling, ppl. a., sense 1, and Baffle, v., senses 6 (to bewilder, from 1649) and 8 (to defeat anyone in his efforts, from 1675); Online Etymology Dictionary, baffle (v.); Agamemnon 1382-1383 (Smyth’s text). The poet’s note, that the sense of defeating efforts came before the sense of puzzling, is not what the dictionary shows and was taken out

notes.note: The same Greek noun names the cloths at the door, at lines 921 and 963. The dictionary gives it there as rug or carpet.
notes.source: Agamemnon 921, 963 and 1383 (Smyth’s text); Liddell-Scott-Jones, heima, sense II: rug, carpet, citing Agamemnon 921 and 963. At line 960 the same noun is used of garments in general (the dye of garments), so that line is not counted

lenses.caption: Two of the translator’s words need their old senses. A trammel was a fishing net before it was any hindrance. Toils are nets for taking prey, and the word comes from the French for cloth, toile. The last line keeps two words of Aeschylus. Abundance stands for ploutos, wealth, and robe for heima, a garment. Both are used at the palace door. The king was loath to waste the wealth of the house, and heima was the word for the cloths he walked on. Auden names the walk as the act that shows the king’s hubris. The robe, named in the same two words, is what holds him for the blow.
lenses.why: Aeschylus names the robe with two words used at the door of the cloths, wealth and garment: the cloths of the walk Auden gives as the king’s hubris and the robe that held him for the blow are named alike.

auden.says: In “The Greeks and Us” Auden also wrote that the tragic hero is a warning, and that the warning is meant for the chorus, the ordinary citizens. At the start of the play the hero has glory and good fortune; by its end he suffers more than they do, because he has run against a law of right that holds for everyone. Watching him fall, the chorus learns that a strong man’s strength tempts him into impiety, which the gods punish. The gods, he wrote, are gods because they are perfectly just, and their strength is the tool of their justice.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 19
auden.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 936-970; read again by the examiner on 2026-10-03, who found each clause of the paraphrase there

auden.says: He added that this world is foreign to a modern reader, who takes a man’s acts to be partly his own free choice and partly his circumstances, and so cannot follow a world where the situation a man is in is enough to make him guilty. The Greek hero, he wrote, is punished for his hubris by being made to sin without knowing it or against his will. His suffering comes on him from outside, as a punishment sent by the gods.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 20–21
auden.checked: read in the same scan, fa.txt, lines 986-991 (page 20) and lines 1032-1037 and 1061-1062 (page 21); read again by the examiner on 2026-10-03 (the page numbers stand at the foot of each page in this scan)

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden wrote that a play of the Greek kind is about an uncommon person who meets an uncommon fate, and that its drama is in what the situation forces that person to do. The chorus may sometimes warn the hero, but he cannot heed them, because a hero of this kind cannot become other than he is.
auden.quote: In a Greek tragedy everything that could have been otherwise has already happened before the play begins.
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 8158-8162 (page 173) and 8234-8238 (page 174); read again by the examiner on 2026-10-03: the running head of page 173 is at line 8148 and that of page 174 at line 8198, and the seventeen words quoted are exact. The examiner reworded two clauses of the paraphrase that ran too close to Auden’s own words

auden.says: In 1945 Auden set the Greek tragic hero beside the Christian one. Greek tragedy, he wrote, is the tragedy of necessity: the spectator pities what could not have been otherwise. Agamemnon is again one of his examples, a hero who must choose between two evils. The hero’s flaw, he wrote, does not produce the tragic situation. The gods send the situation to punish the flaw.
auden.source: “The Christian Tragic Hero,” *The New York Times Book Review*, 16 December 1945, as reprinted in Robert W. Corrigan, ed., *Tragedy: Vision and Form* (1965), pp. 143–44
auden.checked: not seen in a full copy. The wording is in the research notes, remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 2 and appendix block H4, from the 1965 reprint. The examiner found the sentences again on 2026-10-03 in the Internet Archive’s full-text search of that anthology (item tragedyvisionfor0000corr): the sentence on the tragedy of necessity, the sentence on Agamemnon’s choice between two evils (where Antigone is the other example), the sentence that follows it, on the flaw and the situation the gods send, and the anthology’s own acknowledgment, which gives The New York Times Book Review, December 16, 1945; its table of contents puts the essay at page 143. So the newspaper and date no longer rest on memory. That the sentence on necessity is on page 143 and the one on Agamemnon on page 144 is from the research notes; the search does not give page numbers

caveats: The verse and the rhyme are E. D. A. Morshead’s, of 1881. Auden’s list for the course named Louis MacNeice’s translation of 1936, which is in copyright and is not shown here.

No Greek is printed here. What is said of the Greek rests on Herbert Weir Smyth’s text of 1926. Morshead worked from an earlier text and may have read it differently: in the thirteen single lines he has a question and an order where Smyth prints statements.

Auden names Agamemnon for the choice at Aulis and the walk on the carpet. His other sentences used here are about Greek tragedy in general; the page applies them to these lines. His essay of 1945 was read only in snippets of a scanned copy.

The count of nets depends on what is counted. Nine places are counted in Morshead’s English. At one of them the Greek has no net, at one no one is caught, and places that name a robe, a trap or an ambush but no net are left out.
In the translator’s rhymes *took* and *yoke* agree only loosely, and *mind* and *wind* fully only in an older pronunciation of *wind*.
